sn15.1:1.1: This chapter links to the Nidānasaṁyutta through the concept of beginningless transmigration, in which beings are lost because of not understanding dependent origination ([sn12.60:2.3]()).
sn15.1:1.7: Resolve _anamatagga_ as _ana’mat’agga_, where _ana_ is a doubled negative: “no known beginning”. | The idea stems from the the Nāsadīya Sūkta, which twice mentions “in the beginning” (_agre_, Rig Veda 10.129.3, 4; see too 10.90.7, 10.121.1). There, from thought (_manaso_) evolved desire. It concludes, ”This creation—from where it came to be, if it was produced or if not—he who is the overseer of this (world) in the furthest heaven, he surely knows. Or if he does not know …?” (Rig Veda 10.129.7, Jamison/Brereton). Perhaps the Buddha learned the phrase from his former teacher Uddaka Rāmaputta, who at Isibhāsiyāiṁ 23 describes transmigration as _aṇādīyaṁ aṇavadaggaṁ_ (“beginningless, without first point”).
sn15.1:1.8: We encountered a slight variation of this phrase at [sn12.19:1.2]().
sn15.1:1.9: The “Black Plum Tree Land” is _jambudīpa_, the South Asian subcontinent, including India, Pakistan, Nepal, Bangladesh, and Afghanistan.
